prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The five views show a narrow indoor passage opening into a room, with a close wall/partition running through the centre-right and furniture farther ahead; bright lower-edge regions mark the camera wearer’s nearby body or hands, roughly 0.2–0.8 m away, while the floor, doorway and chairs extend about 1–4 m ahead. Across the sequence, the partition shifts from near the right side toward the centre and then left, indicating forward motion combined with a rightward turn around it; the more distant chairs and doorway correspondingly move across the view. The depth map makes the strong near-to-far ordering of body, partition edge, floor and furniture clearer than RGB, but it does not reliably separate similarly dark distant objects or provide trustworthy metric distances. The bright vertical bands at frame boundaries and smooth depth bleeding across wall and object edges are rendering artifacts, and partly visible furniture near the top and side borders has uncertain depth.
descriptions.segmentation: The map consistently isolates portions of the camera wearer at the bottom of the frames, within roughly 0.2–0.8 m, while chairs appear farther ahead at approximately 1.5–3.5 m and a television is detected high on the right in the fifth frame at roughly 2–4 m. Chairs move from the upper-right of the first view to the upper central area in frames 2–3 and then leave the field of view as the wearer advances and turns; the television enters only at the far upper-right in frame 5. The masks make object identity, separation and partial occlusion easier to see than RGB, especially where chairs overlap the background, but they provide little direct information about orientation, facing direction or exact distance. The camera wearer’s fragmented masks are partly cut off by the lower border, several visible furnishings and walls are entirely unlabelled, and the clustered chair masks in frame 3 overlap or fragment, so object count and spacing there are unreliable.
descriptions.pose: Magenta hand skeletons appear near the lower-left or lower-centre in frames 1–3 and 5, placing the camera wearer’s visible hands about 0.2–0.7 m away and within their own arm’s reach; no hand is confidently shown in frame 4. A yellow body skeleton appears only near the upper-centre of frame 3, apparently associated with a distant or poorly localized person-like shape about 2–3.5 m ahead and well beyond the camera wearer’s immediate reach. The pose map clarifies articulated keypoints and limb orientation that are difficult to distinguish in RGB, but the small, incomplete skeletons do not establish gaze direction or whether anyone faces the camera wearer. Missing joints, implausible yellow connections, absent detections in most frames and truncation at the image borders make body orientation, inter-person distance and apparent motion unreliable; only the camera wearer’s hands clearly shift laterally as the viewpoint turns.
